memorial_note: Titanic is the final resting place of about 1,500 people who died on 15 April 1912. Explore with care: observe, photograph and leave the wreck undisturbed.

entries.title: RMS Titanic wreck site
paragraphs: RMS Titanic sank in the early hours of 15 April 1912 on her maiden voyage from Southampton to New York, about two hours and forty minutes after striking an iceberg. About 1,500 of the roughly 2,200 people on board died; published figures range from about 1,496 to 1,523.

The wreck lies about 3,800 m down, some 325 nautical miles south-south-east of Newfoundland. It was found just after 1 a.m. on 1 September 1985 by a French–American expedition led by Jean-Louis Michel (IFREMER) and Robert Ballard (Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution). The towed camera sled Argo, working from the research vessel Knorr, followed a trail of debris until it picked out one of the ship's boilers.

The ship broke apart as it sank. The bow and stern sections rest about 600–700 m apart, and they face opposite ways. Two dense debris fields, each 600–800 m long, trail south-west from the sections, and a thinner scatter spreads over many square kilometres. Most of the debris lies near the stern: boilers, hull plates, fittings, and the personal belongings of passengers and crew.

What you see here: the seabed is real GMRT bathymetry at about 45 x 61 m per cell, which is far too coarse to show the wreck. A full photogrammetric scan made by Magellan in 2022 is proprietary and is not used.

entries.title: The bow section
paragraphs: The forward part of the ship, about 143 m (470 ft) long, stands upright and faces roughly north. It struck the seabed at speed and ploughed about 18 m (60 ft) into the sediment, which buckled the hull. It remains the most recognisable part of the wreck: the forecastle railing, the anchor cranes, the well deck, and the hollow where the bridge once stood.

Iron-eating microbes have been slowly consuming the steel since 1912. They leave rusticles, icicle-like growths of rust that hang from every surface. In 2019 divers in the submersible Limiting Factor found that the starboard officers' quarters, including the captain's cabin and his bathtub, had collapsed. In 2024 an RMS Titanic Inc. survey found that a section of railing about 4.5 m (15 ft) long on the port side of the bow had fallen to the seabed.
In 1986 Robert Ballard left an Explorers Club plaque on one of the bronze-topped capstans on the forecastle deck.

entries.title: The stern section
paragraphs: The stern section, about 107 m (350 ft) long, lies about 600–700 m south of the bow. It sank more slowly than the bow and was far more badly damaged. Air trapped inside burst outwards as it went down, and the impact with the seabed collapsed its decks onto one another. Its hull plating is peeled outwards along both sides.
The stern turned around as it sank, so its rear end now points back towards the bow. The two halves of the ship face in opposite directions.
Hundreds of people were on or near the stern when it went under, because it was the last part of the ship above water. For that reason the 1986 expedition chose it for the memorial plaque.

entries.title: The boiler field
paragraphs: Titanic had 29 coal-fired boilers, each about 4.8 m (15 ft 9 in) across. When the hull broke apart between the second and third funnels, five boilers from Boiler Room No. 1 fell out. They landed as a tight cluster in the debris field around the stern, about 180 m (600 ft) east of it. Because heavy boilers fall almost straight down, the cluster is thought to mark the point where the ship broke up, far above.

One of these boilers was the first object the 1985 expedition recognised. Early on 1 September, Argo's cameras showed its round face and firebox openings on the seabed, and the team knew they had found Titanic.

entries.title: The debris field
paragraphs: As the ship broke apart, thousands of objects fell 3.8 km through the dark water: coal, hull plates, furniture, crockery, bottles, and the belongings of passengers and crew. Heavy pieces fell almost straight down. Lighter pieces drifted with the currents and settled in long trails.

Close to the wreck, two dense debris fields trail south-west from the bow and the stern. Each is 600–800 m long, together they cover about 5 km² (2 square miles), and most of the debris lies near the stern. The 2010 survey by RMS Titanic Inc., WHOI and the Waitt Institute used two REMUS 6000 autonomous vehicles to map the whole site with sonar and cameras for the first time, covering 15–20 square miles (about 39–52 km²) of seafloor. It showed several overlapping debris fields and a much wider scatter, not the single simple trail that had been assumed.
Pairs of shoes still lie where bodies once came to rest. They are among the most moving sights at the site, and a reminder that this is a grave.
This point marks the gap you cross between the bow and stern. The densest debris lies near the stern; the real field is far larger and more varied.

entries.title: Where the "Big Piece" lay
paragraphs: The "Big Piece" is a section of starboard hull plating about 7.9 m wide and 6.1 m high, weighing 15–20 tons. It was part of the wall of first-class cabins on C Deck, extending down to D Deck, and several portholes are still in place. It broke away from the hull and came to rest among the stern-side debris.

First seen in 1994, it was raised by RMS Titanic Inc. in August 1998 after an earlier attempt failed in 1996. It is now on display in Las Vegas. Recoveries like this were controversial, and the international agreement that came into force in 2019 favours leaving the wreck and its artifacts in place.
This point marks the general stern-side debris area where hull plating like this lies. The Big Piece itself is no longer on the seabed.

entries.title: The memorial plaque
paragraphs: In July 1986 Robert Ballard's team returned to the wreck in the crewed submersible Alvin. They fixed a bronze plaque from the Titanic Historical Society to the stern, on the aft starboard side between two fairleads (guides for mooring ropes). It reads: "In memory of those souls who perished with the Titanic April 14-15, 1912." Ballard chose the stern because it was the last part of the ship to go under, and most of the dead were there.
The plaque was gone by 1996, and it is not known what happened to it. Later expeditions left other memorials at the site.

The wreck is protected by the RMS Titanic Maritime Memorial Act (US, 1986), by the Agreement concerning the Shipwrecked Vessel RMS Titanic (concluded in 2003, in force since 18 November 2019), and, since April 2012, by the UNESCO 2001 Convention on the Protection of the Underwater Cultural Heritage. The agreement describes the wreck as a final resting place and favours preserving it where it lies.
No plaque is modelled here. This point marks where it was placed, on the stern.

entries.title: An abyssal channel
paragraphs: The wreck rests on a nearly flat stretch of seabed south-east of the Grand Banks of Newfoundland. The ground varies by only a few metres over hundreds of metres. About 5 km to the north-west, the open survey data shows a shallow channel running roughly north-north-east to south-south-west. It is about a kilometre wide and 50–60 m deep.

Channels like this are cut and kept open by currents and by flows of sediment moving down the continental margin. Deep currents along this margin (the western boundary current and its eddies) also sweep the wreck site itself, sorting the sediment and slowly scouring the debris.
Unlike the wreck, this feature is real survey data from the GMRT grid (about 45 x 61 m per cell). It has no published name that we could find.

facts.label: Relief
facts.value: about 50–60 m below the surrounding seabed
